texts: good. the rule fires whenever a spring tide fills the tide-pools and records the blooming, its location, and its tie to that filling. One thing to watch: the noun 'salt-bloom' reduces to its head word 'bloom' and the verb 'blooms' reduces to the same word, so the substance and the event end up sharing one label — the 'grows' wording in your next sentence avoids that.
good. same rule, cleanly parsed — the tide-pools are one shared set across both clauses, the location sits on the growing only, and every hyphenated term is linked to its head noun.
good. lands as a kind-level description with 'crystalline crust' treated as a kind and 'pale' kept as its own property, so both 'what is salt-bloom?' and 'is salt-bloom pale?' resolve.

mixed: the generic rule is fine, but 'soon' is dropped entirely — there is no slot for imminence, so the parse says salt-bloom dissolves into the seawater without saying how quickly. A manner adverb does have a slot: "Salt-bloom quickly dissolves into the seawater."
